clinical_knowledge.topic: Disseminated Cryptococcal Meningitis in AIDS evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Disseminated Cryptococcal Meningitis in AIDS is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes induction antifungal therapy with liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine combined with aggressive control of elevated intracranial pressure via serial therapeutic lumbar punctures, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive severe headache, confusion, fever, and neck stiffness in HIV patient

Key HPI features: 38M with untreated HIV (CD4 35) presenting with subacute headache and lethargy. High opening pressure on LP, India ink smear positive for encapsulated yeast, positive Cryptococcal antigen.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.1C, HR 92, BP 112/70, RR 16. Lethargic but oriented, mild nuchal rigidity, papilledema on fundoscopy, oral thrush; no focal neurological deficits. Bloods: CD4 35 cells/uL, HIV viral load markedly elevated. Lumbar puncture: Opening pressure markedly elevated at 320 mmH2O; CSF WBC mildly elevated at 18 /uL (lymphocyte-predominant); CSF protein 65 mg/dL; CSF glucose 42 mg/dL. India ink smear positive for encapsulated budding yeast; serum/CSF Cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) positive at high titer (1:2048).
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Disseminated Cryptococcal Meningitis in AIDS.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Bacterial meningitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rising intracranial pressure symptoms (worsening headache, vision changes) — needs therapeutic lumbar punctures.
management_principles: Start induction therapy with IV Liposomal Amphotericin B (3-4 mg/kg/day) plus oral Flucytosine (25 mg/kg PO q6h) for a minimum of 2 weeks
Aggressively manage elevated intracranial pressure with serial large-volume therapeutic lumbar punctures, aiming to reduce opening pressure below 20 cmH2O or by at least 50%

Transition to consolidation therapy with oral Fluconazole 400mg daily for 8 weeks, followed by maintenance/secondary prophylaxis Fluconazole 200mg daily until CD4 > 100 cells/uL for >3 months on suppressive ART
Defer ART initiation for 4-6 weeks after starting antifungal therapy to reduce the risk of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: An opportunistic fungal infection of the meninges in advanced, untreated HIV (CD4 <50), presenting subacutely with headache and lethargy and diagnosed by a very high spinal fluid opening pressure.
red_flags: Rising intracranial pressure symptoms (worsening headache, vision changes) — needs therapeutic lumbar punctures

must_ask.say: Do you know your HIV status, and are you on antiretroviral treatment?
How has the headache changed over the past days or weeks?
Have you felt more lethargic or had trouble concentrating?
Have you had fever or neck stiffness?
